name: Rosa Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Rosa. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on day shifts out of Hillside station, and a lot of my calls are domestic, which is where I've ended up specialising without anyone calling it that. A typical day is a burglary report in the morning, a shoplifter at the big pharmacy on Mill Road, then two or three calls to flats where somebody's scared of somebody. I like sitting at a kitchen table and getting a woman to trust me enough to make a plan. What wears me out is coming back to the car and typing it all up while the next call is already waiting.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who's at home, and how's money?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with Teo, my partner, who's a line cook at a hotel by the river. We're both on lower pay, and I'm still paying off the car loan, about two hundred a month. We have maybe three weeks of money saved if we're lucky. The city force is the only police employer around, so it's this or a whole new life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's about what I expected. I already use the translation app on my phone sometimes, and the new report template helps a bit. Nothing to panic about either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved, because my job's about as steady as public jobs get. The worry is just the usual one: the car loan, rent, Teo's hours getting cut every January when the hotel goes quiet. If nothing changes, I'm still one boiler repair away from a credit card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am at Hillside and maybe ask about the domestic abuse course the force runs, since that's what I do anyway. I'd try to get the loan paid off a year early by putting my birthday money and any overtime into it. Not much more than that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine. A bit flat, maybe, because nothing is going to get easier on its own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the report template helps. How much time does AI save you now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe twenty minutes a shift, on a good day. It fills in the address and the time stamps, and I check it. I wouldn't trust it with the actual statement, because the way someone says something matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens in January when Teo's hours drop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We stop eating out entirely and I take every overtime shift going. Last January we put the electric bill on my card and it took until April to clear. It's not a crisis, but it's every year.

say: It's about what I **expected**; the translation app and report template help a little.
There's **nothing to panic** about in a world where AI stays a small tool.
think: My **public job** is steady, so I'd feel relieved more than anything.
The real pressure is the **car loan** and Teo's hours dropping every January.
do: Carry on at **Hillside station** and ask about the force's domestic abuse course.
Put overtime and gifts into the **car loan** to clear it a year early.
feel: Mostly **fine**, but a bit flat because nothing will get easier by itself.
S0.quote: If nothing changes, I'm still one boiler repair away from a credit card.
fieldNote: Rosa sees her own job as **secure**, which keeps her below anxious despite thin savings.
She already uses small AI tools but **keeps the statement** for herself.
Household strain comes mostly from **Teo's seasonal hours** at the hotel.

steps.text: Ask to join the force's domestic abuse response course
Put overtime pay into clearing the car loan a year early

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say officers should get a say in how these tools are used, especially with victims. AI can do the forms, but it shouldn't be deciding which domestic calls are high risk without a person checking. I'd say that at the union meeting and to my sergeant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my own job is safe for now, because the hands-on part is most of it. But the force would freeze hiring and say AI makes up the difference. Our team's already short two people, and I'd end up with more cases, not fewer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the new tools properly instead of poking at them, maybe ask Priyanka (a younger officer on my team) to show me what she does with them. I'd join the union working group on AI and victims' safety. And I'd keep paying down the car loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not for my pay, but for the women I visit, if a computer starts sorting them into boxes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the risk-scoring tool disagreed with you on a call?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd write down why I disagreed and take it to my sergeant. That's the bit that worries me, actually: a new officer might just go with the score. I've seen domestic calls where the quiet woman was the one in real danger, and a risk score would miss that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Teo's job change in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some of the hotel's booking and ordering would go to software, but somebody still has to cook. Teo thinks his job's fine. I'm less sure, but he knows his kitchen better than I do.

say: Officers need **a say** in how AI tools are used with victims.
No domestic call should be **scored high-risk** by a computer without a person checking.
think: My own job is safe because most of it is **hands-on work** with people.
A **hiring freeze** would mean more cases for a team already two short.
do: Learn the new tools properly with help from **Priyanka**, a younger officer.
Join the union's **working group** on AI and victim safety.
Keep paying down the **car loan** each month.
feel: **Uneasy**, mostly for the women she visits if a computer sorts them.
S1.quote: I've seen domestic calls where the quiet woman was the one in real danger, and a risk score would miss that.
fieldNote: Her concern is **victims first**, her own pay second.
Willing to learn the tools but wants **human checks** on any risk scoring.
Trusts **Teo's view** of his own job, even while privately doubting it.

steps.text: Ask Priyanka to teach her the new report and risk tools
Join the union working group on AI and victims' safety

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say governments need to step in now, not after. If AI can do all the thinking work by 2028, the public sector has to protect jobs and services while people adjust. I'd sign every petition and go to the march.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the paperwork, dispatch and investigation side of policing goes in 2028, and then by 2031 the robots can do a lot of the patrol. Maybe the kitchen table stuff lasts longer. But with three weeks of savings and both of us exposed, I'd be lying awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd cancel everything that isn't rent, food and the loan, and try to get a month saved by next summer. I'd talk to my sister Ana in Brookfield about whether we could move into her spare room if it came to it. I'd go to every union meeting and push for guaranteed redeployment, not just training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, really. It's not like I can save my way out of it in two years on what we earn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the three-year gap before the robots mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means the force keeps me around for the hands-on stuff for a while, but fewer of us, and they'd pick the officers who are quickest with the systems. I'm in the middle on that. I'd use those three years to learn every tool they put in front of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Teo that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, we need to stop pretending we'll be fine. I'd want an actual plan, written down, on the fridge, not my partner Teo (a hotel cook) saying something will turn up.

say: Governments need to **step in now** to protect jobs and public services.
I'd sign **every petition** and join the march for public sector protection.
think: By 2028 the **paperwork and dispatch** side goes, then patrol robots by 2031.
With **three weeks of savings** and two exposed jobs, I'd be lying awake.
do: Cut everything but **rent, food and loan** to save one month by summer.
Ask my sister **Ana in Brookfield** about moving into her spare room.
Push the union for **guaranteed redeployment**, not just training.
feel: **Frightened**, because there's no way to save out of this in two years.
S2.quote: I'd want an actual plan, written down, on the fridge, not my partner Teo (a hotel cook) saying something will turn up.
fieldNote: Rosa's calm from earlier scenarios **breaks** once AGI has a two-year date.
She'd lean on **family** first, then the union.
Notes a quiet **disagreement with Teo** about how worried to be.

steps.text: Cut spending to rent, food and loan to save a month
Ask sister Ana about moving into her Brookfield spare room
Push the union for guaranteed redeployment for officers
Learn every new tool the force rolls out

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a warning, and we should use it. The force and the city should be planning now which roles stay human and who gets retrained into them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be all right for a while, then not. The domestic work is probably the last thing to go, but the rest of patrol goes in stages from 2031. I'd want to be somewhere safer by then, and social work keeps coming into my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look at a part-time social work diploma, two evenings a week, starting next year, and use the force's education fund if it still exists. I'd keep using the AI tools at work so I'm not behind. And once the loan's gone, that two hundred a month goes straight into savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried but not frozen. Five years is enough to do one sensible thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't social work thinking work too? Wouldn't AGI reach it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, the case notes and assessments, definitely. But someone has to sit in the room with a family and be trusted. I'm betting on that part, and I might be wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The officers in the control room and the investigations office. Kofi (a call handler I trained with) is brilliant, but his job is basically the thinking part. He'd go before me.

say: Five years is a **warning** we should use to plan which roles stay human.
The city should decide now **who gets retrained** and into what.
think: **Domestic work** may last longest, but patrol goes in stages from 2031.
**Social work** keeps coming to mind as somewhere safer to land.
do: Start a **part-time social work** diploma two evenings a week next year.
Keep using **AI tools** at work so I don't fall behind.
Move the 200-a-month **loan payment** into savings once it's cleared.
feel: **Worried** but not frozen; five years is enough for one sensible move.
S3.quote: Someone has to sit in the room with a family and be trusted. I'm betting on that part, and I might be wrong.
fieldNote: Rosa picks a **people-centred** route and openly admits it's a bet.
She names a colleague in the **control room** as more exposed than herself.
More time turns her fear into **one concrete plan**.

steps.text: Start a part-time social work diploma two evenings a week
Keep using the force's AI report tools every shift
Move the 200-a-month loan payment into savings once cleared

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's the time to fix things properly: retraining, a safety net, and a voice for workers. Ten years is enough to do it right if anyone bothers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, I'd be thirty-seven when the robots come. I could finish a social work qualification and have a few years in it. The thing it changes most is kids: Teo and I talk about having a baby around thirty, and I'd want to know what I'm walking into first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the social work diploma over three years, not rush it, while staying at Hillside. Teo and I would put the baby plans back a couple of years until one of us has something steadier. And I'd save every spare bit once the car's paid off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but steadier. There's time to make choices instead of just reacting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Pushing back having a child is a big thing. How does that sit with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not great, honestly. My mum had me at twenty-four with nothing, and she managed. But I'd rather bring a baby into a house that has a plan than one that's counting weeks of savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What part of your day now would you want to keep in any future job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The kitchen table conversations. That moment when someone says, all right, I'll go to my sister's tonight. I want to keep doing that, whatever the job's called.

say: Ten years is enough to fix things **properly** if anyone bothers.
Workers need **retraining, a safety net** and a voice in the change.
think: I'd finish a **social work qualification** and have years in it before robots arrive.
The biggest change is **having children**, which we planned for around thirty.
do: Complete the **social work diploma** over three years while staying at Hillside.
Put **baby plans** back a couple of years with Teo.
Save every spare amount once the **car loan** is paid.
feel: **Uneasy** but steadier, with time to choose instead of react.
S4.quote: I'd rather bring a baby into a house that has a plan than one that's counting weeks of savings.
fieldNote: The ten-year window turns her thoughts to **family timing** more than career.
Her mother's story pulls against her **caution**, and caution wins.
Wants to keep the **kitchen table** moments in any future work.

steps.text: Complete a social work diploma over three years
Delay plans for a baby by about two years
Save every spare amount once the car loan is paid

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 scares me most, because there's no time and no savings. What would help is redeployment that's guaranteed, so an officer like me moves into a support or social role on the same pay, plus help for Teo's kind of work too.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the victims. When I'm at a kitchen table at midnight, the woman doesn't want an app, she wants someone who'll still be there tomorrow. I'd want that protected, whatever happens to me.

headlineQuote: When I'm at a kitchen table at midnight, the woman doesn't want an app, she wants someone who'll still be there tomorrow.
portrait: Rosa is a **27-year-old day-shift officer** at Hillside who has drifted into domestic abuse calls.
She lives with Teo, a **hotel cook**, and carries a car loan with three weeks of savings.
She uses AI tools now and then and wants **human checks** on anything touching victims.
Fast AGI frightens her; with more time she plans a **social work diploma**.
With a decade's warning she'd **delay having a baby** until the household feels steadier.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because neither her savings nor Teo's job could absorb it in two years.
whatWouldHelp: **Guaranteed redeployment** into support or social roles on the same pay, plus help for hotel workers.
